nameStory: The six-spotted tiger beetle gets its name from the six pale yellowish or white spots that typically decorate its bright metallic green wing covers, called elytra. The 'tiger' part comes from its fierce predatory nature and lightning-fast reflexes when hunting smaller insects, much like its big cat namesake stalking prey.
description: The six-spotted tiger beetle is a dazzling metallic green predator that looks like a tiny emerald jewel with legs. These active hunters are about half an inch long and spend their days racing across sunny trails and forest clearings in pursuit of smaller insects. Their brilliant green bodies shimmer with an almost mirror-like finish, and they're known for their distinctive zigzag flight pattern when disturbed. As members of the tiger beetle family, they're some of our most spectacular and beneficial insects.

idTips.label: Metallic green color
idTips.description: Body gleams with an intense, mirror-like metallic green that catches sunlight like polished copper or brass - you'll see rainbow reflections shift across the surface as the beetle moves

idTips.label: Six pale spots
idTips.description: Look for six whitish or pale yellow spots arranged along the wing covers - though some individuals may have fewer spots or spots that are quite faint

idTips.label: Large prominent eyes
idTips.description: Bulging compound eyes that look almost comically oversized for the head - they feel smooth and hard if you gently touch them with a finger

idTips.label: Zigzag flight pattern
idTips.description: When disturbed, flies in a distinctive erratic, zigzag pattern for short distances before landing again - never flies in a straight line

idTips.label: Fast running speed
idTips.description: Races across surfaces with incredible speed, stopping abruptly to pivot and change direction - moves almost too fast for the eye to follow

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: About half an inch long with a sturdy, robust build - feels solid and substantial if handled, with strong legs built for running

habitat: Six-spotted tiger beetles love sunny, sandy or bare soil areas where they can easily spot prey and have room to run. Look for them along woodland trails, forest clearings, sandy paths, and the edges of dirt roads where dappled sunlight reaches the ground. They prefer areas with some tree cover nearby but need open patches of exposed soil for hunting.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge in late spring and become active on warm, sunny days. This is peak season for spotting them as they're fresh, brightly colored, and actively hunting.
seasonality.summer: Remain active throughout summer months, though they may be less active during the hottest parts of the day. Look for them in early morning or late afternoon when temperatures are more moderate.
seasonality.fall: Still active into early fall, but numbers decline as adults begin to die off. Colors may appear slightly less brilliant as their exoskeletons age and weather.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off and the species overwinters as larvae living in small burrows in the soil. No above-ground activity during cold months.

funFact: Six-spotted tiger beetles are so fast they can temporarily blind themselves while running - they have to stop periodically to let their eyes readjust and relocate their prey, which is why you'll see them pause in their characteristic stop-and-go hunting pattern.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other metallic green tiger beetles, especially the twelve-spotted tiger beetle which has more spots, or the bronzed tiger beetle which has a more coppery sheen. Remember: six-spotted has that pure emerald green color and exactly six (or fewer) pale spots - count the spots and check that brilliant green shine.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their fierce appearance and predatory lifestyle, tiger beetles are completely harmless to humans and are actually beneficial insects that help control pest populations. Some people mistakenly think they bite, but they're far too small to harm people and are more interested in fleeing than fighting.
compareHints: Among New England's tiger beetles, the six-spotted stands out for its pure metallic green color - the bronzed tiger beetle has more copper tones, while the festive tiger beetle is darker with different spot patterns. The twelve-spotted tiger beetle is similar in color but has more spots, and the purple tiger beetle has distinctly purplish hues rather than green.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's tiger beetles, the Bronzed Tiger Beetle is distinguished by its warm copper-bronze coloration, while the Six-spotted Tiger Beetle shines bright metallic green and the Purple Tiger Beetle displays cooler purple-blue tones.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the festive tiger beetle is distinguished by its particular pattern of white markings and metallic coloration.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the Hairy-necked is the only one with those distinctive fuzzy neck hairs.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the twelve-spotted is unique for having exactly twelve spots on a dark body.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the Oblique-lined stands out with its exceptionally large compound eyes and distinctive diagonal white markings.
Among New England's tiger beetles, the Big Sand Tiger Beetle stands out for its robust, chunky build compared to the more slender Six-spotted or Bronzed Tiger Beetles.
Unlike the bright metallic green Six-spotted Tiger Beetle with its obvious white spots, the Purple Tiger Beetle shows deep purple metallic colors without distinct white markings.

Unlike the Six-spotted Tiger Beetle which prefers woodland paths, or the Bronzed Tiger Beetle found on sandy beaches, the Common Claybank Tiger Beetle is the only New England tiger beetle that specializes in clay habitats.
